title: An Anti-Inflammatory Diet Cut Dementia Risk by 29% — and Your Dadi's Kitchen Had It Right All Along
excerpt: A landmark 15-year study in JAMA Network Open found that diets rich in vegetables, legumes, and whole grains — staples of traditional South Asian cooking — significantly lower the odds of cognitive decline, even in people already showing early signs of Alzheimer's.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • An anti-inflammatory diet can reduce dementia risk by 29%.
  • Traditional South Asian foods align with anti-inflammatory dietary patterns.
  • Ultra-processed foods increase dementia risk by 58%.
  • Whole, minimally processed foods lower dementia risk by 41%.
  • Small dietary changes can significantly impact cognitive health.
Dementia Risk Reduction Through Diet
29%
Lower dementia risk with anti-inflammatory diet
58%
Increased risk from ultra-processed foods
41%
Lower risk with whole, minimally processed foods
24%
Lower risk of cognitive impairment
Source: JAMA Network Open, American Journal of Public Health
For decades, South Asian families have passed down a culinary wisdom that Western science is only now catching up to: load your plate with dal, sabzi, and whole grains, and your body will thank you. A major study published this month in *JAMA Network Open* offers the most compelling evidence yet that they were right — and the stakes may be higher than anyone realized. ## What the Study Found Researchers at Sweden's Karolinska Institutet followed more than 1,800 adults aged 60 and older for up to 15 years, tracking both what they ate and whether they developed dementia. Among participants whose blood tests showed elevated levels of p-tau217 — an Alzheimer's disease biomarker — those who followed an anti-inflammatory diet had a **29 percent lower risk** of developing dementia compared with those whose diets were more inflammatory. The finding held even after accounting for age, education, physical activity, smoking, and other risk factors. The researchers also measured two additional biomarkers linked to nerve cell injury and brain inflammation, finding similar protective patterns. "Our study was observational, so it cannot prove that changing diet will prevent dementia," said Anja Mrhar, the study's corresponding author from the University of Ljubljana and Karolinska Institutet. "That said, the findings are consistent with the broader view that diet quality remains relevant for brain health." ## What Counts as Anti-Inflammatory > **"Leana Wen, a CNN wellness expert and emergency physician at George Washington University, called "an encouraging message" about modifiable risk factors."** There is no single rigid eating plan called "the anti-inflammatory diet." Instead, it describes a pattern: more vegetables, fruits, nuts, legumes, whole grains, and healthy fats, with fewer sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and red meats. The overlap with traditional Indian home cooking is striking. A daily thali built around dal, roti made from whole wheat, seasonal vegetables, and a side of fresh salad or raita checks nearly every box. Spices like turmeric (which contains the anti-inflammatory compound curcumin), ginger, and garlic — foundational to Indian cuisine — have been independently linked to lower markers of chronic inflammation. The study used a tool called the Dietary Inflammatory Index to score participants' diets. People whose scores reflected lower inflammatory potential were consistently less likely to develop dementia — a finding that Dr. Leana Wen, a CNN wellness expert and emergency physician at George Washington University, called "an encouraging message" about modifiable risk factors. ## Why It Matters for the Diaspora South Asians already face a disproportionate burden of cardiometabolic disease. A growing body of research has linked conditions like diabetes and hypertension — more common in South Asian populations — to an elevated risk of cognitive decline. That makes prevention through diet not just helpful but urgent. The challenge is that many NRIs drift away from traditional eating patterns after moving abroad. A reliance on convenience foods, fast meals, and packaged snacks introduces exactly the kind of inflammatory load the study warns against. A separate Harvard study published in June 2026 in the *American Journal of Public Health* underscored the danger: adults who ate the most ultra-processed foods had a **58 percent higher risk** of developing dementia compared with those who ate the least.
Key Dietary Patterns for Brain Health
›Focus on vegetables, fruits, nuts, and whole grains.
›Limit sugar-sweetened beverages and red meats.
›Incorporate spices like turmeric, ginger, and garlic.
›Traditional Indian meals align with these guidelines.
"It really shows there may not be a safe level," said Cindy Leung, associate professor of public health nutrition at Harvard and the study's senior author. Processed meats like bacon and deli meats carried the highest individual risk, while a diet heavy in whole, minimally processed foods showed the opposite pattern — a 41 percent lower risk of dementia and a 24 percent lower risk of cognitive impairment. ## What You Can Actually Do Experts are clear: this is not about perfection or eliminating entire food groups overnight. "Small, sustainable changes — such as eating more vegetables and whole grains, choosing nuts or fruit instead of ultra-processed snacks, and replacing sugary drinks with water — add up over time," Dr. Wen said. For South Asians, that may mean something as simple as cooking more meals at home, leaning into the dietary traditions already in the family repertoire, and being more deliberate about reducing packaged and processed food. Beyond diet, regular physical activity, blood pressure management, adequate sleep, and social engagement have all been linked to better cognitive health in later years. The message from researchers is consistent: dementia is complex, but the lifestyle choices within your control matter more than most people realize. **Sources:** *JAMA Network Open* (July 2026), Mrhar et al.; *American Journal of Public Health* (June 2026), Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health; CNN Health; Medical News Today
